parts.title: UPSC History: The Revolt of 1857 — The First War
parts.intro: Today we study the 'Great Rebellion'. The Revolt of 1857 was the first massive challenge to British authority in India. What started as a sepoy mutiny in Meerut quickly spread into a popular uprising across North and Central India. We explore the multifaceted causes—from the greased cartridges to the Doctrine of Lapse—and the heroic resistance of leaders like Rani Lakshmibai and Kunwar Singh. For UPSC, focus on 'Why the revolt failed' and its 'Long-term Impact' on British policy.

pages.title: Causes of the Revolt
pages.intro: The Revolt of 1857, also known as the Indian Rebellion, had several main causes. The political causes included the Doctrine of Lapse, which was a British rule that let them take over any Indian state whose ruler died without a natural son, and the annexation of Awadh, meaning the British forcibly took control of that large kingdom. The economic causes were heavy taxation that made life very difficult for farmers and the destruction of traditional Indian handicraft industries because cheap British factory goods replaced them. The social and religious causes included the British interfering with local customs, like when they banned the practice of Sati, where a widow was forced to burn on her husband's funeral pyre, and creating fears that the British were trying to force Indians to convert to Christianity. The military causes were the immediate spark of the rebellion: the British introduced greased cartridges for new rifles, which soldiers had to bite open, and the grease was rumored to be made from cow and pig fat, deeply offending both Hindu and Muslim sepoys, who were Indian soldiers in the British army, and there was also a long history of unfair treatment and lower pay for these Indian sepoys compared to their British officers.

pages.title: Centers & Leaders
pages.intro: During the Indian Rebellion of 1857, different cities became centers of the uprising, each led by a key figure. In Delhi, the Mughal emperor Bahadur Shah Zafar was the nominal leader, meaning he was the symbolic head, but the real military command was held by Bakht Khan, a general from the British East India Company's own army. In Kanpur, the rebellion was led by Nana Saheb, the adopted son of a former Maratha ruler, along with his close commander Tantia Tope. In Lucknow, the revolt was organized by Begum Hazrat Mahal, the wife of the deposed Nawab of Awadh. The famous queen Rani Lakshmibai led the uprising in Jhansi, while Khan Bahadur Khan led it in Bareilly. Finally, in Arrah (in present-day Bihar), the rebellion was commanded by the elderly zamindar (landlord) Kunwar Singh.

pages.title: Suppression of the Revolt
pages.intro: The British military suppression of the 1857 Revolt was led by different commanders in key cities. In Delhi, General John Nicholson led the assault that recaptured the city from the rebels. In Lucknow, General Colin Campbell commanded the British forces that relieved the besieged British garrison and later retook the city. In Jhansi, General Hugh Rose led the campaign against Rani Lakshmibai, and he famously called her the "only man among the rebels," meaning he respected her bravery and leadership more than the male rebel leaders. The British used superior weapons, better organization, and brutal tactics, including mass executions, to crush the uprising. By mid-1858, the British had regained control over most of northern and central India, ending the revolt.

items.label: Jhansi
items.value: Hugh Rose (who called Rani the "only man among the rebels")

pages.title: Impact of the Revolt
pages.intro: The Government of India Act of 1858 ended the rule of the East India Company, a private British trading company, and placed India directly under the British Crown, meaning the British monarch. A new official called the Secretary of State, a member of the British government in London, was created to control Indian affairs, and a Viceroy, the Queen's personal representative in India, was appointed to govern the country. The British also abolished the "Doctrine of Lapse," which was a policy that allowed the Company to take over a princely state if its ruler died without a natural heir. Finally, the British intensified their "Divide and Rule" policy, which means they deliberately created or worsened conflicts between different religious and social groups, such as Hindus and Muslims, to prevent them from uniting against British power.
